I think the simple fact of the matter is that with how expensive college is and how hard the job market is, STEM and medical degrees are probably the only ones with a high enough ROI to justify the time and risk invested. I suppose business, finance, econ, and law are good too if you go to a really good school.

No matter how much you love the liberal arts, it's probably a bad idea to spend tens of thousands of dollars learning about it unless you're independently wealthy already. School is one of the largest capital investments you'll ever make and it needs to pay off.

I'd advise liberal arts majors it invest in either a degree with a higher ROI or trade school and study that stuff you love like crazy in your free time. Learning is a great hobby and it's so easy with the internet and great libraries we have. You don't need to pay anyone to learn about awesome stuff.

The way I see it, it is too much of a risk to invest so much money and perhaps take on debt unless you know 100% that you can get a job after graduation.

With some fields of study, there are people who are successful, but the vast majority don't find work in their field.

Classics. Totally worth it.

"But why would you want to learn a dead language?"

Dude, fuck Spanish, L'Anglais is a Germanic language with a 65% Romance vocabulary. Latin teaches you English.

Moreover, I understand the foundations of nearly fucking everything, and because the study of the Classics predates the modern obsession with specialization, I more importantly understand how it all fits together.

Latin got me my first job, and is like a nerd superpower. I fear no jargon. The American constitution is like, 97% cribbed from Polybius.

In terms of money, understanding life, and just plain happiness, I can't recommend a Classical education enough. Most of you were never even offered the opportunity, and you should quite honestly be pissed about it.
